01.missing: The passage reports a ruling, an objection and a reply; no event happens beyond the ruling itself.

02.missing: A sage's statement about his own early marriage; no event is narrated.

03.actor: a half-slave half-free woman and her master
03.event: A woman who was half-slave and half-free was in an unresolved status.
03.turn: The court forced her master to free her.
03.outcome: He made her a free woman.
03.summary: Rabbi Yitzhak reported an incident about a woman who was half-slave and half-free. The court compelled her master to emancipate her, and he made her fully free. The rest is a discussion of whose legal opinion this follows.
03.missing: Why she needed freeing is not stated in the incident itself; [3] offers only a later sage's explanation.

04.missing: A ruling about using a household mortar to secure a door; no event or turn.

05.event: Funerals had become so costly that relatives abandoned their dead and fled.
05.turn: Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in plain linen garments.
05.outcome: Everyone followed his example, and plain burial became the custom.
05.summary: Burials had grown so lavish that the expense was harder on a family than the death itself, and some people simply abandoned their dead and ran. Rabban Gamliel set an example by instructing that he be buried in plain linen. The people followed him, and plain shrouds became the general custom, down to rough cheap cloth in Rav Pappa's day.

06.actor: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya and Rav
06.event: Rav Hinnana taught a version of the mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in Rav's presence.
06.turn: Rav rebuked him for following Rabbi Meir's lone view instead of the Rabbis.
06.outcome: The Gemara explains his reasoning and says he was mistaken.
06.summary: Rav Hinnana was teaching a mishna to Rav's son in front of Rav, and taught it in a strict form. Rav challenged him for abandoning the majority view. The Gemara explains that Rav Hinnana had assumed the whole mishna followed Rabbi Meir, which was wrong.
06.missing: No response from Rav Hinnana; the outcome is the Gemara's analysis rather than an event.

07.event: Rabbi Elazar studied Torah in the lower market of Tzippori while his cloak lay forgotten in the upper market.
07.turn: Someone came to steal the cloak.
07.outcome: He found a serpent guarding it.
07.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah that he would sit studying in Tzippori's lower market while his cloak lay in the upper market. Once a man came to take the cloak for himself. He found a serpent lying on it, guarding it.

08.actor: the daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
08.event: A widow was taking the orphans to court to claim her marriage-contract payment.
08.turn: The orphans, embarrassed by her house clothes, asked her to dress up, so she put on all her clothes.
08.outcome: Ravina ruled that the clothes she wore are appraised and counted against her claim.
08.summary: A widow was suing her husband's orphans for her marriage-contract money. They told her it was shameful for her to come to court in house clothes, so she dressed in all her garments. Ravina then ruled that a widow's clothing on her is appraised, so everything she had put on was counted toward her payment.

09.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave and a gentile woman
09.event: The slave immersed a gentile woman so he could have relations with her.
09.outcome: Rav Yosef said he could declare her and her daughter fit to marry Jews.
09.summary: A slave of Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami had a gentile woman immerse in a ritual bath so that he could be intimate with her. Rav Yosef declared that he could rule both her and her daughter fit to marry into the Jewish community.
09.missing: No turn; the passage moves straight into Rav Yosef's legal reasoning.

10.actor: a man in Eretz Yisrael (in Ilfa's addition)
10.event: A man who longed for a woman wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael.
10.turn: He heard the teaching about the importance of being buried in the Land.
10.outcome: He stayed and suffered there until the day he died.
10.summary: Rabba's brothers wrote to him from Eretz Yisrael, passing on a story from Ilfa. A man was pining for a woman and wanted to leave the Land to go to her. When he heard how much it matters to live and be buried in Eretz Yisrael, he stayed and endured his suffering until he died.
10.missing: The rest of the letter ([3]-[4]) is advice, not narrative.

11.actor: a man from Shot Mishot and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
11.event: A man told the Sages he came from Shot Mishot.
11.turn: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood up and declared that the place lies between the rivers.
11.summary: A man told the Sages he came from a place called Shot Mishot. Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood up and declared that Shot Mishot lies between the rivers, which implied that the man's lineage was sound. The Gemara then explains the legal meaning of the region.
11.missing: What became of the man (for example whether he was accepted for marriage) is not stated.

12.event: A woman wanted to invite her neighbor to come and eat milk.
12.turn: Because of her poor pronunciation she said instead, May a lioness eat you.
12.outcome: The invitation came out as a curse.
12.summary: A Galilean woman meant to say to her neighbor, Come, I will feed you milk. Because she slurred her words, it came out as, Neighbor, may a lioness eat you.

13.actor: Rabbi Hanina Kara and Rabbi Yannai
13.event: Rabbi Hanina Kara sat before Rabbi Yannai and stated that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
13.turn: Rabbi Yannai told him he was wrong.
13.outcome: Rabbi Yannai sent him out of the study hall to recite his verses outside.
13.summary: Rabbi Hanina, a Bible expert, was sitting before Rabbi Yannai and announced that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yannai told him to go outside and recite his verses there, because the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

14.event: Rava publicly taught that straw may be scattered in a rain-damaged courtyard on Shabbat.
14.turn: Rav Pappa challenged him with a baraita requiring an unusual method.
14.outcome: Rava appointed a spokesman and publicly retracted, calling his ruling a mistake.
14.summary: Rava taught in public that one may spread straw over a courtyard muddied by rain on Shabbat. Rav Pappa objected with a teaching that it may be scattered only with the bottom of a broken basket. Rava then had a spokesman stand beside him and announced to everyone that his earlier statement had been his mistake, giving the correct rule.

15.missing: An exegetical explanation of how a biblical determination was made; no narrated event.

16.missing: A hypothetical legal case constructed to explain a dispute.

17.actor: a certain man and Rav Kahana
17.event: A man let witnesses trace their names on ordinary documents, not just divorce bills.
17.summary: A man applied the divorce-bill leniency, letting witnesses who could not write trace their names, to ordinary documents. Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.

18.event: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya, and then died.
18.turn: A man named Toviya came to claim it.
18.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and should receive it.
18.summary: A man on his deathbed said his property should go to Toviya, then died. A Toviya appeared to claim the estate. Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya takes it, without worrying that a different Toviya was meant.
18.missing: Little turn; it is essentially a case report with a ruling.

19.event: A woman told Rava her husband had died in a famine.
19.turn: Under questioning she revealed she had left him with a little flour and only assumed he could not survive.
19.outcome: Rava changed his view and ruled that famine is like war: such testimony is based on assumption.
19.summary: Rava first thought that testimony of death in a famine, unlike war, is reliable. Then a woman came and told him her husband died of hunger. When he asked whether she did right to save herself and leave him a bit of flour, she said, You know a man could not live on that. Rava realized she had not seen him die, and reversed his ruling.

20.missing: A precedent cited as legal proof about how a dowry was collected; no turn or narrative arc.
